source1: G.P. Malalasekera, Dictionary of Pali Proper Names, s.v. 'Kulasekhara' and 'Ariyacakkavatti', Pali Text Society 1937-38 - https://palikanon.com/english/pali_names/ku/kulasekhara.htm
notes: Pandyan general Ariyacakkavatti, under Kulasekhara (r. 1268-1308), sacked Subhagiri after Bhuvanekabahu I and took the Tooth Relic; Parakkamabahu III later retrieved it. Pandyas were Shaivas (Hindu); no sign they adopted Buddhism.

conqueror_tradition: Other: Yuezhi steppe nomadic religion (poorly attested)
source2: Han-period texts on the Yuezhi and Daxia (Hirth and Wylie transl.), Silk Road Seattle, University of Washington - https://depts.washington.edu/silkroad/texts/hantxt1.html
notes: Yuezhi nomads (customs 'same as the Xiongnu') took Bactria c. 130 BCE and copied Greek predecessors' coinages (Greek legends, deities); no evidence of Greek cult at court. Bactrian population partly Iranian. Pre-conquest writing not attested.
Buyids were Shi'ite Daylamite military leaders; Ahmad (Mu'izz al-Dawla) entered Baghdad in December 945 and kept the Abbasid caliphs for Islamic legitimation. Shi'a and Sunni count as one tradition.

source1: Michael Lobban, 'Indirect Rule in West Africa and the Paradoxes of Secular Imperialism' (review of R. Akande, Entangled Domains, Cambridge UP 2023), Rechtsgeschichte - https://rg.lhlt.mpg.de/index.php/rg/article/download/2342/2446?inline=1
notes: Britain conquered the Sokoto caliphate (Muslim state from dan Fodio's 1804-08 jihad) in March 1903; Lugard pledged not to interfere with Islam and excluded Christian missionaries, ruling via emirs. British rulers stayed Christian.
Latin (Western) Christian crusaders took Constantinople in 1204 and installed Baldwin of Flanders; the conquest deepened the Orthodox-Catholic schism. Catholic and Orthodox count as one tradition.

source2: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Great Living Chola Temples' - https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/250
notes: Pallava dominions passed to the Cholas c. 880 (Britannica; database says c. 897 under Aditya I). Pallavas backed Brahminical faith, Mahendravarman I became Shaiva; Chola kings built Shiva temples, Saivism deeply rooted. Both Hindu.

source1: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Ten Lost Tribes of Israel' - https://www.britannica.com/topic/Ten-Lost-Tribes-of-Israel
notes: Assyria conquered the northern kingdom c. 722/721 BCE and its tribes were assimilated. Conquered tradition is Israelite Yahwism (ancestor of Judaism); Assyrians practiced Mesopotamian religion (Ashur). No evidence Assyrian kings adopted Yahweh worship.

source1: United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, 'The German Churches and the Nazi State', Holocaust Encyclopedia - https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/the-german-churches-and-the-nazi-state
source2: Anita Bunyan, review of R. Steigmann-Gall, The Holy Reich (Cambridge UP 2003), Times Higher Education - https://www.timeshighereducation.com/node/85125
notes: Almost all Germans were Catholic or Protestant; the Nazi platform endorsed 'positive Christianity'. Steigmann-Gall argues many Nazi leaders saw themselves as Christian, against the older anti-Christian/pagan view; contested, so low confidence.

Adil Shahis established Shi'ism at Bijapur with Persian as court language; Qutb Shahis were Shi'ite with strong Persian influence. Both stayed Muslim until Mughal annexation (1686-87). Britannica dates Vijayanagara's final collapse c. 1614, not 1646.

source1: Emanuel Beska, 'Muhammad Ali's Conquest of Sudan (1820-1824)', Asian and African Studies 28(1), 2019 - https://www.sav.sk/journals/uploads/0521120903_BESKA_final.pdf
notes: Ismail Kamil Pasha's expedition took Sennar in June 1821 and Badi VI surrendered; Muhammad Ali was a Muslim Ottoman viceroy ruling for the sultan-caliph. Britannica's Funj dynasty page calls it an Islamic empire.
